highlight.text: he states that the ancient painters were in the habit of daily making a painting of both a Shinto and a Buddhist deity as an offering and [invocation] to each. For this reason, he says, he for many years made a practice of executing every morning one painting of the Buddhist goddess Kwannon

work.text: To those who associate [Kyōsai’s] style of painting merely with his [caricatures] and hasty humorous productions, this selection of a master by pious students of the highest style of religious art may appear somewhat incongruous.

source.author: Josiah Conder

work.lead: Conder, on the two Buddhist priests who studied with him:

moment.text: In addition to his caricatures, Kyōsai painted a large number of pictures and sketches, often choosing subjects from Japanese folklore, Noh plays, nature, and religion, for example The Temptation of Shaka Niorai or The Goddess Kwannon on a dragon (on kakejiku frame).

matters.text: Because this Bodhisattva is considered the personification of compassion and kindness, a mother goddess and patron of mothers and seamen
matters.lead: Kannon is the Japanese name of Guanyin, the bodhisattva of compassion:

matters.text: She is usually portrayed in statues and painting as a young woman dressed in a white robe which sometimes covers the head, acting as a veil.
